data.title: Postal Service to make fuel surcharge permanent in 2027
data.description:
(NewsNation) – The U.S. Postal Service announced it will raise domestic shipping prices, making the fuel surcharge permanent in 2027. 

USPS said that it will make a temporary 8 percent surcharge, which was first implemented in April of this year, permanent, with an additional 3 percent “given the recent further elevation of fuel prices.” 

The surcharge will reportedly be reevaluated in July 2027 based on fuel prices in the first half of 2027. 

The Postal Service also filed a notice to increase prices for USPS Ground Advantage, Priority Mail, Priority Mail Express and Parcel Select. The change would raise domestic shipping service prices by 5.9 percent on average, according to a news release. 

USPS added that it is also changing international mail and shipping rates, raising prices by an average of 7.9 percent for some services. 

“The USPS governors believe these new rates will keep the Postal Service competitive while providing the agency with much needed revenue as it continues to struggle with financial issues,” the agency said in a statement.

data.title: FDA issues recall for honey dietary supplement over undeclared ED ingredient
data.description:
(NewsNation) — A California-based company has recalled its honey dietary supplement after an undeclared ingredient used to treat erectile dysfunction was discovered in its products.

Eros Apothecary said its Candy Power For Man Organic Honey product contained tadalafil, according to a notice issued by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

“The recall was initiated after FDA laboratory testing identified undeclared tadalafil,” the notice said.

“Consumers should stop using Candy Power For Man immediately and dispose of any remaining product,” it continued.

The FDA said the product was sold on eBay between April 27 and July 20, and came in yellow and orange packaging.

Anyone who has experienced health issues after using the product should consult their healthcare provider, the notice stated.

data.title: Vance, Rubio top 2028 list for Republicans, Ossoff and Buttigieg get nod in polling of Democrats
data.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President Vance lead a new survey of Republican voters on whom they view as a strong presidential candidate in 2028.

With midterms in the rear view, both parties are already beginning to look to the next presidential election.

In a new Reuters/Ipsos poll, 45 percent of Republican voters said Rubio would make an excellent candidate for president, with another 23 percent saying he would be a good candidate. Only 5 percent said he would be a poor choice.

The vice president was not far behind, with 43 percent rating him an excellent candidate, and another 28 percent rating him as good. Vance has long been considered the frontrunner, and recent actions suggest he may be trying to distance himself from unpopular positions of the administration. After the midterms, he was quick to blame the Iran war for GOP losses.

In third place is Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, with a combined 60 percent saying he would be excellent or good, but a sharp drop off emerges after that.

President Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr. is in fourth place, but views of him are very polarized — 38 percent rated him a poor candidate, more than the combined share who said he would be excellent or good. The president’s approval rating in the Reuters/Ipsos poll held steady at a near-record low 32 percent, which may hurt his son’s perception among Republicans.

On the Democratic side, the nomination appears to be wide open, as several candidates have moderate levels of support. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff led the pack, each with 29 percent saying they would be an excellent candidate. Another 27 percent say Buttigieg would be good, and 20 percent say the same of Ossoff.

Buttigieg, former mayor of South Bend, Ind., ran in 2020, where he performed unexpectedly well, narrowly winning the Iowa caucus. Ossoff is seen as a top contender after winning reelection in battleground Georgia by nearly 20 points.

Still, more than a third of Democratic voters have not heard of him or skipped rating him. More than 20 percent said the same of Buttigieg.

In third place is a candidate nearly all voters had heard of but had polarized views on: 23 percent said former Vice President Harris would make an excellent candidate, and another 30 percent said she would be a good one. But a combined 45 percent say she would be fair or poor, the most of any candidate surveyed on the Democratic side.

The top six candidates on the Democratic side would all likely classify themselves as moderates, and the only progressive on the list is Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), with 15 percent saying she would make an excellent candidate, and another 33 percent saying she would be good.

No major candidates have yet announced for president, but historically, candidates have announced in the weeks and months after the midterm elections. In 2022, Trump announced his comeback bid just one week after the midterms.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted Nov. 6-9 among 477 registered Republican voters and 538 registered Democratic voters. The margin of error is 5 points.

data.title: Bobby Pulido wins Latin Grammy days after winning House race
data.description:
After defeating GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in the Lone Star State’s midterm elections last week, Texas Rep.-elect and Tejano musician Bobby Pulido (D) won his third Latin Grammy on Thursday evening. 

He topped the award ceremony’s “Best Tejano Album” category for his project “Bobby Pulido & Friends: Una Tuya y Una Mía (Vol.2/En Vivo).”

Just days before his win, he was up on Capitol Hill for new member orientation. The Washington Sun reported that he was among the newly elected lawmakers who missed a traditional House freshman class photo because he was en route to the award ceremony in Las Vegas. 

During his acceptance speech on Thursday evening, Pulido shared that he was retiring from the music industry. 

“I want to tell you that I’m retiring from music, and I’m leaving with so much gratitude,” he said in Spanish. 

He added, “I’ll see you soon, because we need to represent and we need to get to work to use our voices for something else.” 

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) congratulated Pulido on his win in a social media post. 

“Last week @PulidoForTexas crushed his MAGA opponent and flipped a Republican House seat,” Jeffries wrote. “This week he just won a Latin Grammy Award for Best Tejano Album. Felicidades and what a month for Congressman-Elect Pulido.”

Pulido said on Tuesday that he would not bring his Grammy to Washington, D.C., if he won the album nomination, telling TMZ’s Charlie Cotton, “This is a place for work.”

“It’s a much bigger responsibility to be a public servant than it is to be a singer, for sure, no doubt,” he said. “Your decisions really affect people, and as a singer you can influence people in a different way, but it’s not the same.”

While the representative-elect said he was setting aside his professional career, he told Cotton he spoke with Florida Rep. Darren Soto (D) during orientation about joining a band made up of members of Congress. 

“I think they’re recruiting me,” he told TMZ. “They need a vocalist, so we’ll see.”

data.title: Democratic Sen.-elect Flanagan backs Van Hollen over Schumer
data.description:
Democratic Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota announced Friday that she’s backing Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) in his challenge to Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to become Senate majority leader next year.

“Minnesotans are demanding change. Democrats need to deliver. That starts with new voices in our leadership. I believe @ChrisVanHollen is the leader and fighter we need to bring about real change, so no American is left behind,” Flanagan said in a statement posted on X.

Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, beat centrist Rep. Angie Craig (D-Minn.) in a competitive primary before going on to win the general election against former sportscaster Michelle Tafoya, the GOP nominee.

Van Hollen endorsed Flanagan in the Senate Democratic primary, as did other Senate progressives such as Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).

Flanagan called for “radical change” during the Democratic primary, such as “ripping apart” Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and passage of Medicare for All to provide universal health care coverage.

Schumer threw his support behind Craig in the primary.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) of Michigan has also said he plans to support Van Hollen, who also backed him in the Michigan Senate Democratic primary over Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), who had Schumer’s support.

Van Hollen announced his intention to challenge Schumer in a social media post Thursday evening.

“In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn’t about any one person – it’s about answering that call. That’s why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader,” he posted on X.

data.title: Public safety is a rare bipartisan win Congress shouldn't let slip away
data.description:
The midterm elections are finally over. The campaign texts have stopped, the attack ads are off the air (and our feeds), and Americans can at last put months of political angst to bed. Or, so we hoped.

Another election season has come and gone, but the partisan tension lingers. It isn’t a new feeling, but it is increasingly a roadblock to good policy that improves Americans’ lives. However, Congress now has a real opportunity to set that tension aside and deliver meaningful public safety solutions through a package of bipartisan bills.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Ranking Member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) have offered a set of public safety bills as amendments to the National Defense Authorization Act. Together, they show what a thoughtful, targeted approach to crime looks like, tackling online child sexual exploitation, organized retail crime, and contraband in federal prisons.

Their approach? Address each problem narrowly and specifically, so the policy actually moves the needle on community safety. Rather than piling on punishment for its own sake, the bills aim for consequences that fit the threat and are serious enough to hold offenders accountable for reprehensible conduct.

Government’s first duty is to protect the most vulnerable among us, especially children. That responsibility does not disappear when crime moves online. Sextortion, which means coercing someone into sending sexually explicit images, often by threatening to expose them, can reach any child with an internet connection. In 2024 alone, the FBI received nearly 55,000 sextortion complaints, a 59 percent jump from the year before.

Federal law has not kept pace. The proposed James T. Woods Act, named for a victim of online sextortion, would update federal sentencing laws for child sexual abuse material. It would also create two new crimes targeting sextortion and violent online networks like 764, which coerce children into harming themselves or others. The goal is simple — hold predators accountable and ensure fewer children become victims.

Additionally, law-abiding citizens and businesses also should not bear the cost of organized crime. Organized retail theft is not petty shoplifting. It is driven by sophisticated networks that operate across state lines, raising prices and putting workers at risk. Because these schemes cross jurisdictions, the federal government has a role to play. The Combating Organized Retail Crime Act would strengthen the federal response by creating a multi-agency task force, improving coordination between retailers and law enforcement, and giving authorities new tools to recover stolen goods.

Public safety also extends behind prison walls. Incarceration should protect the public and prevent further crime, not give offenders a way to keep operating from their cells. Contraband cell phones let inmates continue directing criminal activity on the outside. The Lieutenant Osvaldo Albarati Stopping Prison Contraband Act would make possessing a contraband phone in federal prison a felony rather than a misdemeanor. What happens inside prisons can feel out of sight, out of mind. But safe, secure prisons are essential to public safety, officer safety, and the integrity of the justice system.

Critics may argue these proposals are just another push for tougher penalties, that public safety belongs to state and local authorities, or that crime bills don’t belong in a defense bill. Those concerns deserve thoughtful consideration, but they should not distract from the problems at hand. Online exploitation, interstate theft rings, and federal prisons are inherently federal challenges. And the National Defense Authorization Act, which has passed every year for more than six decades, is one of the few reliable vehicles in what feels like a gridlocked Congress.

The real question is not whether a policy sounds tough, but whether it offers a targeted, effective response to serious criminal conduct. Today, sizable gaps in federal law leave children exposed, let criminal networks profit, and allow offenders to keep operating behind bars. These bills close those gaps.

In a climate in which distrust of the political process seems to be at an all-time high, lawmakers should seize every chance to show that protecting the public is a shared priority. This is one of those chances. Congress should keep this package in the final National Defense Authorization Act and not let the moment slip away.

Rachel Wright is the National Policy Director for Right On Crime.

data.title: Live updates: Van Hollen gains support in challenge to Schumer; Outlook starts bouncing back
data.description:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) announced Thursday night he will challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to become the majority leader of the upper chamber next Congress, as Schumer faces dissent from new senators in particular.

“I think that we heard loud and clear from the American people that they want to end the war in Iran and bring down prices,” Van Hollen told MS NOW’s Jen Psaki. “We should do it now. We shouldn’t say we’re going to wait till January.”

As of Friday, he appears to have support from Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), Sens.-elect Peggy Flanagan (Minn.), Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.), Annie Andrews (D-S.C.), Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Troy Jackson (D-Maine).

appeared together at a news conference on Tuesday and said they would not back Schumer. Some incoming senators said the same, including Sens.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.), Annie Andrews (D-S.C.), Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Troy Jackson (D-Maine).

Microsoft’s catastrophic Outlook outage started easing on Friday morning, more than 18 hours after it turned off email for millions of people.

The Federalist Society on Thursday night heard from Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito at its annual convention. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will address the group Friday night. Alito implored Congress to fund the high court and chastised lower judges for sometimes issuing “unjustified” orders blocking presidents’ policies.

The East Potomac Park lawsuit returns to a Washington courtroom on Friday, two weeks after a federal judge opened an investigation into concerns that the Trump administration lied to her in the ongoing legal battle over President Trump’s desire to redevelop the golf course there.

Trump has a series of policy meetings at the White House on Friday.

Follow live below.

data.title: Trump 'gaslighting' over Huang controversy: Kara Swisher
data.description:
Left-leaning journalist Kara Swisher criticized President Trump’s response to outgoing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal involving an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, saying the president is downplaying the seriousness of the allegations.

“He has to say nothing’s going on here … because if there were, he’s in real trouble,” Swisher told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins in a Thursday interview. “This is serious national security issues, and to pretend that it’s not a big deal is kind of ridiculous. It’s gaslighting, you know, which is what he does all the time whenever something happens.”

Huang resigned as CEO of the chipmaker and tech giant Thursday after reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman named Alice Huang, whom the U.S. government suspected of being a spy for the Chinese government.

Trump has mostly stood by Huang, calling him an “honorable man” and saying the situation was “sad,” though he said in an interview Thursday that if the woman is indeed a spy for China, then Huang was right to resign. 

The New York Times reported Thursday that Trump called Huang and told him to fight for his job.

The Times previously reported that Trump was told twice about Huang’s relationship with the woman and her suspected connections to China, but did not appear to do anything with the information. Two months after the first time he was notified, he reversed course and allowed Nvidia to sell its highly-advanced chips to China.

Now, members of both parties are calling for an investigation.

Multiple House Republicans have said they want Huang to brief them behind closed doors on his relationship with the woman and potential security concerns, while some Democrats want to look into what Trump knew and what he did about it.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Jim Banks (R-Ind.) have called on Congress to pass their bill restricting Chinese access to advanced chips like Nvidia’s.

Swisher told Collins that there needed to be an investigation in Congress and that she did not trust the administration to look into the matter given Trump’s involvement.

“[Trump is] trying to throw doubt in a situation that requires real investigative work, which I don’t expect from either Todd Blanche or Kash Patel,” Swisher said. “It’s up to Congress to really look at this. And it looks like the Republican senators are at least taking national security issues seriously.”

Even if Republicans do not agree to look into it in the next few weeks, Democrats’ big midterm wins will put them into comfortable majorities in both chambers starting in January, where they will control investigations and have subpoena power. 

The incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), has already said he wants to pursue investigations of Trump and his allies. The White House vowed to respond aggressively.

data.title: White House staff to need prior approval to meet with lobbyists, under Stephen Miller memo
data.description:
A new memo from White House chief of staff Stephen Miller says White House staffers need prior approval from the Office of White House Counsel if they want to meet with a lobbyist, a significant shift after the midterm shellacking of the GOP.

“No President in history has fought more relentlessly, selflessly or courageously for the American People than President Trump. Following his example, White House staff are expected to dedicate their time unwaveringly to the working people of the nation,” the memo states.

The memo says the prior approval covers meetings on the White House complex with registered lobbyists related to government policy.

A White House official said the memo was sent out last night and is a “much stricter process than before.”

It also says the Office of Public Liaison will continue to serve as the primary point of contact for engagement with external stakeholders.

Politico first reported the memo.

Republicans lost the House and Senate majorities in last week’s elections, with Democrats winning Senate seats in such previously red states as Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Mississippi.

While the elections were focused on the economy, affordability and the Iran war, corruption was an underlying theme of the campaigns.

Trump named Miller as his chief of staff on the Friday after the elections. Miller replaced Susie Wiles, who had come under criticism from some administration officials over her ties to lobbying groups.

Former senior health adviser Calley Means criticized Wiles as a career lobbyist concerned only with catering to corporate interests. He claimed Wiles and her former deputy chief of staff James Blair stunted the “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) agenda by siding with corporate donors ahead of the midterm elections.

“Just as a statement of economic facts; Susie Wiles, her career has been taking money from the industries and foreign governments who would pay her the most money. That’s what she did. Nobody disputes that,” Means said while on the “Joe Rogan Experience” podcast last week.

Means resigned last month from the Department of Health and Human Services over frustrations with the lack of MAHA advancements.

The White House has pushed back on the allegations, saying the administration “has never allowed and will never allow outside groups to influence policy decisions.”

“President Trump is busy executing on his America First agenda that includes the largest working-class tax cuts in history, over a million private sector jobs added to the economy, a sealed shut border, and lowest violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said in a statement.

data.title: Democrats won, now we need to deliver
data.description:
In the aftermath of 2024, experts were arguing not about whether Democrats could retake the U.S. Senate in 2026, but if we ever could. Forecasters projected Republicans holding at least 53 seats in the midterms, including North Carolina.

But because of candidates laser-focused on lowering costs for families in their state, as well as Republicans’ massive failure to tackle high prices and the corruption in Washington, we made history.

In North Carolina, Sen.-elect Roy Cooper (D) not only flipped a state President Trump carried all three times, but he did it by competing in suburban, exurban and rural areas — winning 21 counties Trump carried in 2024. By expanding the map and fighting to earn every vote, Cooper provided coattails that flipped an incredible five congressional seats, the state House and broke the state Senate supermajority. These historic victories, in potentially ten states that Trump carried, are worth celebrating. But we can’t take our foot off the gas, and we can’t fall into the same traps that previous midterm winners have fallen into. Democrats also need to take a clear look at ourselves.

Democrats may have carried the night on Tuesday, but 57 percent of Americans still have an unfavorable opinion of our party. As much as there is to celebrate, we should be clear-eyed that Tuesday was more about Republicans losing than it was about the national Democratic brand carrying us to victory. If we look at how Cooper or Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.) won, it was by talking about diesel, not about being a Democrat.

Working families are sick of the chaos and corruption that has crushed their budgets and left them struggling to afford the basics. On Tuesday they gave Democrats a chance. Now, we need to deliver.

Cooper ran on a simple, catchy slogan: Make stuff cost less. He did not get distracted by shiny objects or hot-button issues that the D.C. political class was spinning themselves up about day after day. He talked about what voters were experiencing every single day: high prices. His message resonated not because it drove clicks or viral moments but because it was rooted in making daily life for everyday people easier.

Cooper vowed to not become a lobbyist and refused to own or trade individual stocks, so that North Carolinians knew that he would focus on their wallet, not his own. If we fail to deliver for these folks, 2028 will be the same as 2026, 2024 and 2020 — an election where voters hit the change button yet again.

Instead of ceding ground on crime as far too many folks in our party do, Cooper proudly ran on his record keeping families safe by putting violent criminals behind bars, going after drug dealers, opposing defunding the police and strengthening bail laws as attorney general and governor.

This is the path Democrats must take in order to win in 2028 and bring the American Dream back within reach for so many families: talk like normal people and work to make groceries cheaper.

Delivering results for families doesn’t mean we roll over to this administration. Because of how Trump has weaponized tariffs to reward his cronies, families are paying more at the grocery store. Because of how this administration has started a reckless war, families have paid record fuel prices for months and Americans have been killed. 

Accountability is important, not for the sake of getting even, but for the sake of delivering a better life for working people. But if we take our eye off the main goal of lowering costs, if we become more preoccupied with evening the score then lowering the grocery bill, we won’t have done any good for families who entrusted us with their vote and are still struggling to get by.

Voters spoke loud and clear on Tuesday. We have some power, again. And with that power comes responsibility. But we cannot confuse us winning with them losing. If we want to win in the future, if we want to win in 2028, we can’t let this opportunity go to waste: we have to focus on the issues that matter and deliver a more affordable future for families across this country.

Morgan Jackson was a general consultant on Roy Cooper’s campaign and senior advisor to Cooper.
